extraction.citation: Jiang Y, Zheng X (2014). Private sector participation and performance of urban water utilities in China. Economic Development and Cultural Change 63(1):155-189.
extraction.service_provider: 208 large and medium urban water utilities, state-owned or with private (nonstate) shareholders
extraction.regulatory_model: private sector participation (PSP) in urban water supply: opened to private investors on a pilot basis in 1992 and nationwide in 2002; PSP defined as any nonstate capital contribution, PSP majority when nonstate sources hold more than 50% of capital; water tariffs are heavily regulated by the government (public hearings required for tariff changes)
extraction.population: urban water utilities of prefecture-level cities (192 cities; 188 with population data had more than 900 million inhabitants and about 300 million urban residents in 2007)
extraction.sample_size: Balanced panel of 208 urban water utilities in 192 cities, 1998-2007, from the National Bureau of Statistics Annual Industrial Firm Surveys (firms with sales above CNY 5 million; water production and supply; large and medium utilities in prefecture-level cities); about a third had private shareholders by 2007, two-thirds of those with a majority. Table 8: 814 utility-year observations for the domestic-supply and domestic-population outcomes, 1,752 for total urban water supply
extraction.effect_measure: fixed-effects panel regression with lagged utility variables and city controls (Arellano-Bond dynamic models for some outcomes); coefficients on log outcomes, standard errors clustered at utility level
extraction.effect_estimate: Table 8 (all columns with lags and city controls). Domestic water supply population (log), N = 814: PSP 0.026 (SE 0.025) in the original coding and 0.037 (0.026) in the corrective recoding; PSP majority 0.032 (0.026) original and 0.046 (0.026, p < 0.10) in the corrective recoding, PSP minority 0.006 (0.034) and 0.015 (0.038). The authors read the 0.046 as an average 4.6% increase in the domestic water service population under majority private ownership against state-owned utilities. Urban domestic water supply (log), N = 814: PSP -0.054 (0.044) and -0.044 (0.052); PSP majority -0.071 (0.038, p < 0.10) original and -0.062 (0.047) corrective. Total urban water supply (log), N = 1,752: PSP -0.020 (0.026) and -0.038 (0.030); PSP majority -0.040 (0.030) and -0.055 (0.035). The authors call the effects 'either statistically insignificant or marginally significant' and the picture 'still pretty vague', and read the supply declines as possible leakage reduction. Elsewhere PSP majority cut employment by about 12% and raised the profit-sales ratio by 7.1 percentage points (Table 7, col. 6), which the authors attribute to efficiency rather than tariff increases.
extraction.extraction_sample_size: 814 utility-year observations (domestic-supply outcomes); 208 utilities in 192 cities
extraction.adjusted_or_unadjusted: adjusted (utility fixed effects, lagged utility variables, city controls)
extraction.covariates: utility fixed effects; lags of utility variables; city control variables (population, road infrastructure and others); PSP probability modelled from lagged utility and city variables
extraction.study_design: quantitative panel-data analysis of utilities (observational; exposure is a change in ownership, not a trial)
extraction.risk_of_bias_rating: Serious for the household-access outcome (appraised 2026-10-13 on the full text against ROBINS-I; Domain 1 confounding: Moderate (utility fixed effects, lags and city controls, a model of PSP probability, but selection into PSP on profitability is acknowledged); Domain 2 selection: Low (utilities matched across years by name, size, location and manager; balanced panel); Domain 3 classification of interventions: Moderate (PSP from capital-source codes, 27 corrective recodings, results shown for both codings); Domain 4 deviations: not applicable; Domain 5 missing data: Moderate (domestic outcomes cover 814 of about 2,000 utility-years); Domain 6 outcome measurement: Serious (domestic users and domestic supply are recovered from industrial-survey variables, not a coverage or connection measure); Domain 7 selection of reported result: Moderate (two codings and three PSP definitions reported; estimates marginal))
extraction.measurement_bias: Serious (the domestic service population is derived from industrial survey variables)
extraction.confounding: Moderate (fixed effects and controls; time-varying selection into PSP on profitability acknowledged)
extraction.attrition: Moderate (814 of about 2,000 utility-years have the domestic outcomes)
extraction.reporting_bias: Moderate (several codings and definitions; marginal significance)
extraction.legal_measurement_quality: moderate (ownership from capital-source codes; majority and minority split; 27 corrective recodings; no direct measure of the regulatory regime)
extraction.outcome_measurement_quality: low (domestic water service population is derived from industrial survey variables, not a household coverage or connection measure)
extraction.source_document: Jiang & Zheng 2014, Economic Development and Cultural Change 63(1):155-189
extraction.table: Tables 6-8 (Table 8: impact of PSP on urban water supply)
extraction.section: Full text (journal article, 35 pages): Introduction; Literature; Data and Variables; Empirical strategy; Results (PSP drivers, performance, Table 7 majority v minority, Table 8 water supply and users); Conclusions
extraction.exact_location: Data and Variables (pp. 160-162: 208 utilities, 192 cities, PSP definition); Table 8 and the text before it (pp. 183-184); the one-third and two-thirds private-share figures (p. 156 and p. 183)
extraction.extraction_note: New inclusion by the PI's A16 adjudication of 2026-10-13 (narrow reading of criterion 2: utility ownership and regulatory structure directly governing service access; the original E06 exclusion had rested partly on the access estimate being non-significant, which is not an exclusion criterion, open item A18), extracted from the full-text PDF in the researcher's Drive (35 pages read as text, tables read from the text layer). The abstract and introduction say 200 cities; the Data section gives 208 utilities in 192 cities. The codebook's mechanism columns have no ownership flag, so no rule-type flag is set; ownership and tariff regulation are recorded under regulatory_model. The effect row in effect_sizes.csv is a reasoned non-fit (see its provenance note).

evidence_map.evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a fixed-effects panel of 208 Chinese urban water utilities in 192 cities (1998-2007) estimating the effect of private sector participation on utility performance and, in Table 8, on domestic water supply and the domestic service population (N = 814 utility-years; marginal significance, domestic users derived from industrial-survey variables); read in full text 2026-10-13.
evidence_map.institutional_context: urban water utilities opened to private investors on a pilot basis in 1992 and nationwide in 2002; government-regulated tariffs
